steps.text:

  - structured logging: model identifiers, timestamps, request/response pairs
  - anomaly detection over telemetry -> unexpected behavior
  - synthetic monitoring: predefined test prompts sent repeatedly (e.g. after model/prompt update) -> regressions

  - human-in-the-loop review at important checkpoints
### Open source tools and standards
- new field -> open standards/tools to avoid tying telemetry to one vendor
- most notable: OpenTelemetry (Cloud Native Computing Foundation project) semantic conventions for generative AI
  - common way to record model calls, token usage, tool and agent calls, evaluation scores; telemetry readable across tools
  - still under active development, not yet stable
- open source instrumentation libraries emit telemetry following conventions automatically for common providers/frameworks
- separate open source projects for tracing/evaluating ML and LLM apps; some export/import OpenTelemetry format -> work with general purpose backends, not just own dashboard
- table of representative open source tools
  - OpenTelemetry, MLflow: ML-oriented
  - Prometheus, Grafana: general-purpose metrics/visualization backends
### Proprietary platforms
- commercial managed services combining tracing, evaluation, monitoring
- table of representative vendors, not exhaustive
### Agent observability
- often a distinct sub-area: multi-step workflows, autonomous decisions, external tools -> more complex execution paths than single-prompt calls
- evaluation (can agent do task, before/during deployment) vs observability (is it performing correctly once deployed)
- tracing as hierarchy of spans: model invocation, tool call, memory access, sub-agent delegation = child spans of request
  - latency, cost, error state per step; find which step produced incorrect/unsafe intermediate result
- capturing intermediate reasoning before an action = distinct signal; shows why, not only what

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Some of the techniques that are associated with AI observability are the following:

End to end tracing of requests as they go through pipelines, chains, or agent steps, so that every stage of the execution can be seen.

Structured logging of events, which includes model identifiers, timestamps, and request and response pairs.

Anomaly detection over the telemetry, to surface behavior that is unexpected.

Synthetic monitoring, where predefined test prompts are sent again and again, for example after a model or prompt update, to detect regressions.

Automated evaluation, which includes using one language model to assess the output of another one, which is often called "LLM-as-a-judge", for qualities that are hard to measure with conventional code.

Human-in-the-loop review at important checkpoints.

### Open source tools and standards
- new field -> open standards/tools so telemetry not tied to one vendor
- most notable: OpenTelemetry (Cloud Native Computing Foundation project) semantic conventions for generative AI; record model calls, token usage, tool/agent calls, evaluation scores; one tool's telemetry readable by another
- still under active development, not yet stable
- instrumentation libraries generate conventions-compliant telemetry automatically for common providers/frameworks
- open source tracing/evaluation projects for ML and LLM apps; some export/import OpenTelemetry format -> general purpose backends, not only own dashboard
- table: OpenTelemetry, MLflow ML-oriented; Prometheus, Grafana general-purpose metrics/visualization backends

### Proprietary platforms
- commercial managed services integrating tracing, evaluation, monitoring
- table of representative vendors (not exhaustive)

### Agent observability
- distinct sub-area: multi-step workflows, autonomous decisions, external tools -> more complex execution paths
- evaluation (can it do the task, before/during deployment) vs observability (performing correctly once deployed)
- hierarchy of spans: model invocation, tool call, memory access, sub-agent delegation as child spans; per-step latency, cost, error state; find step with incorrect/unsafe intermediate result
- intermediate reasoning before action as separate signal: why, not only what

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Some of the techniques that are associated with AI observability are the following:

End to end tracing of requests as they go through pipelines, chains, or agent steps, so that every stage of the execution can be seen.

Structured logging of events, which includes model identifiers, timestamps, and request and response pairs.

Anomaly detection over the telemetry, to surface behavior that is unexpected.

Synthetic monitoring, where predefined test prompts are sent again and again, for example after a model or prompt update, to detect regressions.

Automated evaluation, which includes using one language model to assess the output of another one, which is often called "LLM-as-a-judge", for qualities that are hard to measure with conventional code.

Human-in-the-loop review at important checkpoints.

### Open source tools and standards

AI observability is a new field, so several open standards and open source tools have been created so that telemetry is not tied to a single vendor. The most notable of these efforts is the semantic conventions for generative AI that are defined by OpenTelemetry, which is a Cloud Native Computing Foundation project. The conventions describe a common way of recording model calls, token usage, tool and agent calls, and evaluation scores, and this means telemetry produced by one tool can be read by another tool. The conventions are still under active development and they are not yet marked as stable.

There are open source instrumentation libraries that can generate telemetry following these conventions automatically for common model providers and frameworks. Separately there are several open source projects that focus on tracing and evaluating machine learning and LLM applications, and some of them can export or import data in the OpenTelemetry format, which lets them work together with general purpose observability backends and not only with their own dashboard.

The following table lists representative open source tools that are used in AI observability pipelines. OpenTelemetry and MLflow are oriented specifically toward machine learning workloads. Prometheus and Grafana are general-purpose tools, and they commonly serve as the metrics and visualization backends that the AI-specific components export data to.

### Proprietary platforms

Several commercial platforms offer AI observability as a managed service, and they integrate tracing, evaluation, and monitoring into a single product. The following table lists representative vendors, but it is not exhaustive.

### Agent observability

Observability of autonomous agents is often treated as a sub-area of its own. This is because agents navigate multi-step workflows, they make autonomous decisions, and they invoke external tools, so the execution paths they produce are more complex than the ones from single-prompt model calls. Practitioners distinguish between evaluation, which tests if an agent can perform a task before or during deployment, and observability, which monitors if it is performing correctly once it is deployed.

Tracing an agent execution is typically structured as a hierarchy of spans. Each model invocation, tool call, memory access, or delegation to a sub-agent is a child span of the request that encloses it. With this structure the latency, cost, and error state of each individual step can be examined in isolation, and it becomes possible to identify which step in a multi-step pipeline produced an intermediate result that was incorrect or unsafe. Capturing the intermediate reasoning that an agent produces before it commits to an action is also treated as a separate telemetry signal, because it lets operators assess not only what the system did but also why it chose to do it.
